title: Chapter 1. When barter gave way to money: your work for 4 coins

blocks.text: There is an ancient gesture that can still be understood without words. One person brings what they have made with their hands — a jar, a loaf, a handful of fish just taken from the lagoon — and the other brings theirs. They look at each other. If the deal is fair, no scales are needed: it is enough that both sides recognise each other. That was barter. It was not a paradise. Sometimes one went away hungry and the other with more than they needed. But in that exchange a face still fitted. Things were exchanged; the person was not bought.

blocks.text: Then came an idea that seemed small and was not: your work, for four coins.
blocks.html: Then came an idea that seemed small and was not: your work, for four coins.

blocks.text: Four coins fit in the fist. They weigh almost nothing. They do not smell of bread or of salt. They do not break if they fall to the ground, or they break in another way, more silently: they are spent, lost, owed. And yet, from a moment in history, those pieces of metal began to say how much a whole day of a life was worth. The potter no longer handed over the jar in exchange for the fish. They handed over the jar in exchange for a number. With that number, if it stretched, they bought the fish from a third person. The face faded behind the figure.

blocks.text: This chapter tells of that shift. Not in order to dream of a past that will not return — no one here asks that we go back to swapping goats for knives in the square — but in order to understand how a person's effort became a quantity, and how that quantity, money, sat down in the middle of the table and has not got up.

blocks.text: Schoolbooks often say that first there was barter and that barter was awkward, and that that is why coin was invented. The history is longer and more honest. Before anyone stamped a face or a lion on a piece of metal, there was already a way of measuring work and debts. In Mesopotamia, more than four thousand years ago, temples and palaces kept accounts on clay tablets. They measured barley, wool, silver. A shekel of silver — the šiqlu, a unit of weight of about eight and a third grams — served to value different goods and also to value the work of whoever was not master of their own day. Barley was everyday money, the money of rations and of bread. Silver was the money of larger dealings, of merchants and of debts that were dragged from one harvest to the next.

blocks.text: That was already money, even if it was not yet coin. It was a measure. And a measure, when it is applied to a person, ceases to be only a tool: it becomes a judgement. “So much have you worked, so much is yours.” The sentence seems reasonable. In part, it is. The problem begins when the “so much” fits into four coins and a whole life is organised in order to get them.

blocks.text: In the Code of Hammurabi, from around the eighteenth century before Christ, wages in silver and rations in barley are already fixed for those who work for another. A field hand, a boatman or a day labourer has their work priced at a quantity. There is no need to quote every article here as if this book were a treatise. It is enough to see the gesture: the effort of a body, under the sun of Babylon, turned into a weight of metal or a volume of grain. Barter still existed, of course. People went on exchanging what they had. But, beside that exchange, another custom had been born: paying for work with a measure that was not the work itself, nor the fruit of the work, but its equivalent in a metal that shone and could be stored, lent, demanded.

blocks.text: There lies the egg of what would later be the wage. There were still no coins in the pocket. There was already, however, the idea that a day's work has a price.

blocks.text: Coin, the kind that can be counted on the fingers — one, two, three, four — came later. Historians and numismatists agree, with the nuances any origin requires, in placing the first minting in the kingdom of Lydia, in the west of what is now Turkey, in the seventh century before Christ. They were pieces of electrum, an alloy of gold and silver that the river Pactolus washed down towards Sardis, the capital. They were not round and perfect like those of today. They had the shape of a bean or a small ingot, a regular weight and, newest of all, a mark: often the head or the paw of a lion, the sign of the royal house. That mark was a promise. It said, in silence: this piece of metal is worth what power says it is worth. It was no longer necessary to weigh the silver at every deal, or to trust only the colour of the metal. It was enough to count.

blocks.text: Herodotus, who wrote his Histories in the fifth century before Christ, attributed to the Lydians, “the first of the men we know,” the having minted and used coin of gold and silver, and also the having been the first to take up retail trade. He was writing centuries after those first pieces, and he spoke of gold and silver, when the earliest were of electrum. The science of coins has refined the story: Lydian electrum, towards the end of the seventh century; later, in the sixth, under Croesus, the separation of gold and silver into distinct coinages. The nuance does not deny the idea. It only denies haste. What matters, for this book, is not to win a dispute about dates. What matters is the change of custom: suddenly, or almost suddenly, value fitted in the palm of the hand and had a stamp.

blocks.text: With coin, barter did not disappear altogether. It has never disappeared altogether. There is always someone who swaps a favour for a favour, a basket of figs for a repair, a help for a help. But coin prevailed because it was light, divisible, recognisable. It could be saved. It could be owed. It could be demanded. And, above all, another person's work could be paid for with it without handing over anything one had made. Four coins, and until tomorrow.

blocks.text: That “until tomorrow” is graver than it looks. In barter, the deal ends when the two things have changed hands. In work for coins, the deal never ends: tomorrow the same day must be sold again, and the next, and the next. The coin is spent. Hunger is not. Thus was born, without any need for a single decree or an inventor with a first name and a surname, a way of life in which a human being does not exchange what they have created, but hires themselves out for a handful of metal.

blocks.text: Pedro is fond of the Phoenicians. He names them with affection, as one names distant relatives of whom one is proud. And he is right to look at them closely, because they understood the Mediterranean as a long table, with ports instead of plates, and because their trace reaches this district, the Mar Menor and Cartagena.

blocks.text: The Phoenicians, coming from the cities of the Levantine coast — Tyre, Sidon, Byblos — travelled the sea with timber, purple, glass, metals, ivory and everything a mercantile people knows how to set in circulation. For centuries they traded without needing to mint their own coin. They weighed the metal. They exchanged goods. They founded or encouraged trading posts and cities along the shores, and one of them, Carthage — Qart-ḥadašt, the New City — became a power of the western Mediterranean. The traditional date of its foundation, at the end of the ninth century before Christ, lives beside what archaeology has gradually made more precise: a clear rooting in the ninth and eighth centuries. The essential thing is not the exact year. The essential thing is the craft: to go, to return, to deal, to know languages, not to stay shut on a single shore.

blocks.text: Coin came to them as well, later than to Lydia and the Greek cities. Carthage minted, especially from the fifth and fourth centuries before Christ, and did so with more intensity when armies, alliances and crossings had to be paid for. The horse, the palm tree, the image of Tanit: pictures still recognised in museum cases today. Coin, which had been born as a convenience for the market, also revealed itself as a tool of power. Whoever mints, commands. Whoever pays in coins organises the work of many who do not know one another.

blocks.text: And here, beside the lagoon, that history touched land.

blocks.text: Long before this coast was called what it is called, there was already trade. There are Phoenician wrecks in these waters — those of Mazarrón, the cargo of Isla Grosa — that speak of lead, of tin, of commerce in the seventh century before Christ. In the fourth century, beside the Mar Menor, at Los Nietos, an Iberian settlement served as a stop: products of the mining sierra were exchanged for goods from Greece, from Campania, from the eastern Mediterranean. It was still, in large measure, a world of exchange and of weight. Coin circulated little.

blocks.text: Around 227 before Christ, Hasdrubal the Fair founded on a formidable harbour a city he again called Qart Hadasht: New City. Today we call it Cartagena. In the name he wanted a sister of Carthage. At its back were the sierras of silver and lead, that wealth that had drawn merchants for centuries. With the metal of these mountains, coin was struck. The Hispano-Carthaginian coins of those years — silver shekels, pieces with ships' prows, with effigies and symbols — were not an ornament. They served, among other things, to pay those who worked and those who fought. A person's effort, once again, fitted into a few coins. The Mar Menor, so close, looked on without saying anything: water is not minted. Water is shared or lost, but it cannot be saved in a sack.

blocks.text: That capture is not told here in order to praise a war. It is told because the place where Pedro writes, and from which he looks at the lagoon, is made of that memory: Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Romans, miners, fishers, people who first bartered and then counted coins. The landscape remembers what the pocket forgets.

blocks.text: Imagine, for a moment, a man or a woman of those shores, more than two thousand years ago, at the end of a day. They have loaded, rowed, cut stone, baked, spun. Four coins are placed in their hand. They count them. They are cold. They bear a horse, or a face, or a symbol they did not choose. With them they will be able to buy bread, if bread has not gone up. They will be able to owe less, or owe more, according to the day. What they will not be able to do is recover the sun that has gone into the work. The sun is not kept in a sack. The coins are. And because they can be kept, tomorrow they will be asked to hand over the sun again in exchange for another four.

blocks.text: That is the operation this book calls, with the harshness of the title, the devil's invention. It is not work. Work, when it consists in making, caring, repairing, fishing, teaching, accompanying, is one of the most dignified ways of being in the world. The invention is another: turning that making into a commodity, and that commodity into a handful of metal, and that metal into the measure of the person. “You are worth what you earn.” “So much you work, so much you are.” Four coins, and be silent.

blocks.text: Barter, with all its limits, still tied value to a visible thing. Money unties it. It makes it abstract. A coin does not say who sweated for it. It does not say whether the day was long, whether the body hurt, whether the deal was fair. It only says a number. And numbers, when they accumulate, begin to command those who do not have them.

blocks.text: That is why the passage from barter to coin is not a museum anecdote. It is the moment when work stopped looking at the face and began to look at the price. Mesopotamia measured it in shekels and in barley. Lydia stamped it in electrum. The Phoenicians and Carthage carried it across the sea, and at Qart Hadasht, a step from the Mar Menor, the metal of the sierra became coin and the coin became a wage. Since then, with variations that seem huge and belong to the same family — the denarius, the maravedí, the peseta, the euro, the balance on a screen — we go on doing more or less the same thing: handing over a life in instalments, in exchange for a number that evaporates.

blocks.text: Four coins. The number is Pedro's, and it does not pretend to be a historical quotation of a price. It is an image. It is the size of what we are given for what is taken from us. Few coins, much day. Little thing, a whole back. Anyone who has worked for a wage that does not stretch, or for one that stretches and still leaves a taste of having been priced, understands the sentence without having it explained.

blocks.text: The past should not be idealised. Barter did not save anyone from need. In the palaces of Mesopotamia there were rations and there were hierarchies. In the mines of these sierras there was, centuries later, fatigue and wealth badly shared. Coin did not invent inequality. It gave it a unit of account, a way of carrying it from one place to another and of inheriting it without having to inherit the flock or the field. It made it liquid, as people say now. And what is liquid seeps in everywhere.

blocks.text: Nor is the point to hate coins as one hates an enemy. A coin is an object. The problem is not in the object. It is in the custom of measuring with it what should not be measured that way: dignity, time, care, the lagoon, the health of a community, the right not to be a price. When money becomes the only language, the other languages — that of craft, of help, of the gift, of beauty that is not sold — grow hoarse.

blocks.text: That is why this book begins here, at that crossroads between barter and the four coins. From Lydia to Cartagena, from the clay tablets to today's purse, the question is the same: who decided that a person's day is worth so little, or so exactly that, and no more? No one decided it all at once. It was decided gradually. It was accepted. It was taught as if it were nature itself, when it was only an invention: useful, powerful, and, if left alone, capable of eating us whole.

blocks.text: On clear nights, from the Mar Menor, the glow of Cartagena can sometimes be seen. The new city of the Carthaginians is still there, with another name and other noises. Under the streets there are coins that no longer circulate, that no longer buy anything, that only serve to remind us that the metal lasts longer than the day labourer. The water, by contrast, is still water. It has no mint. It has no obverse or reverse. Whoever bathes in it does not pay with anyone's face.

blocks.text: Perhaps that is why it is worth looking back at barter not as a recipe, but as a memory: that of a deal in which the other person could still be seen. And it is worth looking at the four coins not as a fatality, but as a habit that can be discussed. The chapters that follow — the humanoids that work for humans, the coupons for what is necessary, a world in which being a millionaire no longer gives power, and the ways out Pedro imagines with artificial intelligence, with a politics that is not a trade of command, with the Moon, with the garden, with travel in the virtual and with the account of how we arrived at a society of people living alone — are born of that discussion.
